pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Walk me through `schema.graphql`. What are `Query` and `Mutation` doing there, what does the `!` in `[Comment!]!` mean, and what does "schema-first" mean as a workflow rather than a file format?
expected_points: the schema is the contract both sides agree on, written in SDL, before any code
Query is the root of every read and Mutation the root of every write; a third root, Subscription, streams events
`!` is non-null: `[Comment!]!` is a list that is always present and never contains a null, though it may be empty
non-null is operational, not decoration: a failing non-null field propagates null up to the nearest nullable parent, and with none the whole response becomes data: null
schema-first means generating Go types/interfaces from the SDL and implementing the holes, so the compiler enforces the contract; code-first derives the schema from structs and nobody reviews it

questions.prompt: A GraphQL server does not execute a query — it executes a tree of fields. Explain what that means, using the resolver signature from the exercise, and say what one resolver call does and does not know.
expected_points: a resolver is func(ctx, parent, args) (any, error): one field, one parent object
Query.posts runs once and returns five posts; Post.title then runs five times, Post.author five times
each call knows only its parent and its own arguments — not its siblings, not how many times it is about to run, not the rest of the query
that ignorance is what makes arbitrary client queries possible and is also where every performance problem comes from

questions.prompt: The naive `Post.author` resolver is one correct line and it is the bug. Explain the N+1 problem it causes, why you cannot fix it with a join, and how the exercise proves it is fixed.
expected_points: one query for the list plus one per post for its author: five posts, six store calls; five hundred posts, five hundred and one
the schema shows nothing — `author: Author!` says nothing about what it costs
no place to put a join: the resolver runs per parent and never sees the sibling posts
the fix is a dataloader, and the tests count store calls: one AuthorsByIDs with three distinct ids versus five AuthorByID calls
make performance claims you can assert as a number

questions.prompt: Describe your `Loader`: what `Load` does, what `Dispatch` does, and how the executor knows when to dispatch without a timer.
expected_points: Load fetches nothing: it records the key and returns a pending *Result handle
the same key twice returns the same *Result — dedupe and per-request cache in one map
Dispatch takes the queued keys, clears the queue, calls the batch function exactly once (WHERE id IN (...)), and fills in every result
empty queue means no call at all; a batch error goes to every key; a key the batch did not return gets a per-key error wrapping ErrNotFound while its siblings resolve
the executor resolves one level at a time and dispatches at that boundary; a resolver returns a Deferred the executor forces after dispatch
production loaders use a short time window instead, which makes batching tests a race against a timer

questions.prompt: You already have body-size limits, rate limiting and timeouts from the hardening lesson. Why does a GraphQL endpoint still need depth and complexity limits, and why do you need both?
expected_points: those bounds assumed the server decides what an endpoint does; here the client sends the work in a small body over one URL, and the rate limiter counts one request
depth bounds a cyclic schema — Post.author.posts.author... is legal and unbounded — and is cheap and blunt
complexity estimates cost before execution: weight times parents, with a list field multiplying the parent count for its children by `first` or by the field's default page size
neither subsumes the other: the deep cyclic query with first:1 is complexity-cheap, and `{ posts(first: 5000) { title } }` has depth 2
both run before the first resolver — a rejected query touches the store zero times, answers 400 and carries no data key
the default page size is the important half: an unbounded list field looks free to the analyser and returns the whole table at runtime

questions.prompt: Your response has a `data` key with a null in it and an `errors` array — and the status is 200. Explain that, and say which failures are *not* 200.
expected_points: GraphQL answers a tree, and parts of a tree fail independently: the client gets everything that resolved plus an errors array with a path naming exactly what did not
200 because the request was understood and executed — the failure is in the data, not the transport
a client that only checks resp.StatusCode renders a half-empty page and reports success; that is the most common GraphQL client bug
a request that never executed — unparseable, unknown field, over the limit — is a request error: 400 with no data key at all
resolver errors should be mapped to a safe message plus a machine-readable code in extensions, not echoed verbatim

questions.prompt: Give me one API you would build with GraphQL and one you would refuse to, and defend both. What does GraphQL cost you that REST does not?
expected_points: reach for it when many different clients need different shapes of one graph, the data really is a graph, and the organisation can govern the schema as a reviewed artifact
refuse it for a public read-heavy API where CDN and browser caching are doing real work — one URL and a POST body give a cache nothing to key on
also refuse for one client you control, a handful of endpoints, or a payload that is not a graph (uploads, streaming, bulk export)
costs: no free HTTP caching, unknown per-request cost that must be estimated and bounded, batching as a permanent obligation, clients reading two response keys, a tooling floor above curl
the practical middle: `/posts?include=author,comments` fixes under-fetching for many services
the expensive mistake is adopting GraphQL without loaders, limits and schema review — a REST API with worse caching and unbounded cost

questions.prompt: Someone proposes making the loaders a package-level singleton so the cache survives between requests. What do you say?
expected_points: the loader's cache is a per-request identity map, not a cache: it promises two reads of a key inside one query agree, and nothing more
shared across requests it is a cache with no invalidation, serving stale rows
worse, in an API where authorization decides what each caller may see, a stale entry hands one user another user's row
it would also need locking, because requests are concurrent — the single-goroutine assumption is what lets the exercise's loader skip a mutex
the exercise asserts this: two identical requests must cost two batch calls

questions.prompt: You have lost HTTP caching and `IN (...)` with 5,000 ids is its own outage. What do you do about each?
expected_points: caching moves into the application: per-request loaders, a shared object cache keyed by entity, or a CDN-friendly path via GET for queries
persisted queries: clients register queries at build time and send an id, which turns arbitrary-query risk back into a fixed endpoint list and restores cacheability
loaders take a maximum batch size, and every list field is paginated so the analyser has something to charge
complexity limits are the bound that makes a batch size predictable in the first place
field-level usage tracking plus @deprecated is how a field is retired without a /v2
